text: An AI pilot has finished and the review queue is moving faster. The manager asks, can we expand?
Open the agreement the team made before the pilot.
This fictional scorecard covers forty eligible pull requests before the pilot and forty during it.
Count each request once, even when several reviewers worked on it.
Both groups cover the same service, eligibility rule, and follow-up after merge.
Expansion requires the time benefit and every guardrail to clear. Keep that agreement in view.
Open one request. Start the clock when the author marks it ready. Stop at the first human comment that examines the change.
A bot check or a quick acknowledgment leaves the clock running. Use working hours on the team calendar.
Sort forty waits from shortest to longest. Average the twentieth and twenty-first values.
Repeat for the other group. The baseline median is eighteen business hours.
The pilot median is thirteen.
Five fewer business hours at the median. Thirteen clears the fourteen-hour target.
How much time did a reviewer spend reading?
For that, we need another measure.
Switch to active review. These are the minutes spent reading and evaluating a request.
The hours spent waiting belong to the first measure.
The median was twenty-four minutes before and twenty-six during the pilot.
Effort rose two minutes. The pilot is one minute inside the agreed ceiling of twenty-seven.
Carry both observations into the meeting. The queue was shorter in this sample, and the typical review took a little more work.
Staffing or the mix of changes may also have differed between the two periods.
Count a request once when a reviewer asks for a material change to behavior, tests, or scope.
Three comments on that request still count as one case. A spelling correction alone falls outside this definition.
Six of the forty baseline requests needed rework. That is fifteen percent.
In the pilot, seven of forty needed rework. Give yourself a moment to divide seven by forty.
Seventeen and a half percent.
One additional request moved the rate two and a half percentage points above the fifteen-percent ceiling.
Keep the counts beside the rates.
Each group saw one post-merge defect in the same follow-up window.
Record one out of forty in each. With two events altogether, we have little basis for a claim about a defect trend.
Open the ledger. One hundred dollars for licenses, twenty for the approved workspace, and one hundred and twenty for training.
Add the three entries. The total is two hundred and forty dollars.
The agreed cap is three hundred dollars. That leaves sixty.
Divide the total by forty eligible requests and you get six dollars per request.
Reviewer labor is still measured in minutes here. Pricing that labor would require an agreed rate.
Time and spending clear their thresholds. Rework misses, and the pilot recorded zero serious data or access incidents.
What would you change?
Start with the seven requests behind the missed guardrail.
Read the review reason beside the changed files. The ticket asks for a validator fix.
The diff also changes an unrelated configuration file. The reviewer asks the author to remove it.
Four of the seven cases show that pattern.
Recommend one adjustment. Ask authors to name their intended files and check the final diff against that scope.
Retest in the same service with the same thresholds. The pattern suggests a change to try.
It cannot tell us what caused the difference between periods.
Try a fresh hypothetical cohort. Fifty eligible requests. Eight needed material rework.
The ceiling is fifteen percent. Assume every other guardrail and the time target are met.
Pause here. What is the rework rate?
What is the largest whole number of reworked requests that would still meet the ceiling?
Write both answers, then name one piece of evidence you would want before recommending a change.
Eight out of fifty is sixteen percent. Seven out of fifty is fourteen percent.
Seven is the largest whole count that meets the ceiling.
Would you prescribe the same fix again?
We have only a count. Read the review requests and their diffs.
If they reveal a correctable pattern, propose one change and retest.
If the cause remains unclear, investigate before choosing the intervention.
A defensible update can be short. Eight of fifty requests needed rework, above our agreed limit.
We will hold expansion and examine those eight cases before choosing the next step.
